findings.title: Vectorized/GPU-compatible force interface cannot express the force model it is required to run
findings.description: The document requires "The hot loop must be structured for vectorized computation over arrays of agent state, not object-by-object iteration" (Design Goals, "Efficient large-scale evaluation") and, in "GPU compute path for force accumulation", requires the force interface to remain "bulk array-in/array-out operations with no Python-level per-agent branching, no dynamic allocation, and no callbacks into Python during the hot loop." The same document's force model requires per-agent variable-length neighborhoods ("For each active agent, queries nearby neighbors through the spatial query interface"), and the pluggable-spatial-query principle only constrains *strategy*, not the shape of neighbor results. Ragged, per-agent neighbor sets inherently require a Python-level loop to assemble and per-agent allocation, which is precisely what the GPU constraint forbids and what the documented per-agent call pattern produces. No mechanism is named for bridging this: no padded-neighbor matrix, no CSR/flat index+offset representation, no fixed-capacity top-K neighbor scheme. This is the document's largest unaddressed complexity cliff, and it is not merely future: slices 100 and 101 are already complete with a Python loop over agents (see `src/migratory/engine/flocking.py` and the per-agent `query_radius` loop in `src/migratory/engine/tick.py`), so the "tens of thousands of agents at full behavioral fidelity on a single CPU process" goal currently has no supporting design. Related: "Array layout for vectorized computation" defers SoA vs AoS as "needs validation against the actual force computation patterns" even though "Data-oriented agent state" in Architectural Principles already asserts contiguous typed arrays as settled, and no slice in the plan carries any performance acceptance criterion, so the scale goal is never validated.

findings.title: Environment is described as an input parameter and as a queried interface
findings.description: Envisioned State, step 1 says the tick "Receives the current agent state array, environmental context, and an optional active-agent subset." Architectural Principles, "Environment as input surface", says the opposite: "The engine queries environmental state (terrain elevation, resource locations, threat zones, seasonal parameters) through a read-only interface." Design Goals ("Clean boundaries") lists "environmental queries" as an engine-exposed interface. These are three different contracts — a value passed in per tick, a queryable object the engine calls, and an engine-owned interface surface — and the consequences differ materially (who calls whom per agent, whether terrain sampling is pull-based per agent or pre-sampled into arrays). The world server document compounds this by asserting the environment layer "provides terrain elevation, biome data, resource locations, and seasonal state to the behavior engine through a read-only query interface." Pick one, and state how per-agent environmental sampling interacts with the vectorization requirement above (per-agent Python calls into an environment object would re-introduce exactly the hot-loop pattern the doc forbids).

findings.title: Swarm/stigmergy archetype is not producible by the scoped engine, yet it is a Design Goal and is missing from Anticipated Slices
findings.description: Design Goals requires "visually and statistically distinguishable movement patterns for each behavioral archetype (flocking, herding, pack hunting, territorial/solitary, swarm intelligence) from shared underlying mechanics with different parameter weights", and Architectural Principles asserts "Profile-driven behavior — All behavioral variation comes from parameterized profiles, not from archetype-specific code paths." But Envisioned State states "Swarm agents respond to environmental stigmergy (reinforced paths) rather than direct neighbor forces" — that is not a reweighting of cohesion/separation/alignment/attraction/repulsion/flight; it requires agents to *write* environmental markers. Architectural Principles simultaneously forbids this: the environment interface is explicitly "read-only" and the engine "does not own or manage environmental data." So the archetype cannot be built by the engine as scoped. The consequence is visible downstream: the 100 slice plan defers swarm intelligence to Future Work (106), gated on the Environment Layer initiative, and "Anticipated Slices" in this document omits swarm (and migration) entirely. The document should either drop swarm from the archetype-fidelity goal or state explicitly that the fifth archetype requires an engine↔environment write channel that is out of scope here, and move it out of "shared underlying mechanics with different parameter weights."

findings.title: Aggregates cannot be presented through the neighbor query interface as described
findings.description: "Multi-resolution simulation and aggregation" claims "the engine may need to evaluate forces between individually-simulated agents and nearby aggregates, which the world server would present through the same neighbor query interface." The interface described throughout is a point query — "which agents are within radius R of agent A" — returning agents that live in the state arrays. An aggregate is not an agent: it is a statistical descriptor (center of mass, heading, dispersion radius, count) with no entry in `positions`/`velocities`/`profile_indices`, and it has spatial extent, so a point-in-radius test is the wrong predicate (an individual can be inside the aggregate's dispersion radius without being near its center of mass). The world server slice plan (108, "Aggregation Interface Support") repeats the same assumption. Nothing in this document defines how a heterogeneous neighbor result is represented, or how a strictly-index-based neighbor contract would carry aggregate descriptors and aggregate-scaled forces. As designed, this extension point forces a rewrite of the neighbor query contract rather than composing with it.

findings.title: Profile abstraction conflates per-agent parameters with pairwise interaction parameters
findings.description: "Inter-archetype interactions" correctly identifies that "an elk herd member's separation force from a nearby wolf is qualitatively different from its separation force from another elk" and that "Profile-to-profile interaction rules add a combinatorial dimension to the parameter space." But Architectural Principles defines a profile as "a set of named weights, ranges, and thresholds" on the profile itself, and Design Goals promises "Adding a new species or creature means defining a new profile, not writing new simulation logic." Pairwise directional rules (prey's response to predator ≠ predator's response to prey; pack target selection) are n×n relations, not per-profile scalars, so they cannot live in a single flat profile without duplicating rules into every profile or encoding profile identity inside a profile. The document raises the problem and then defers its resolution entirely; the profile data structure is the document's headline extension point, so leaving its representation of pairwise rules undecided is a load-bearing gap rather than a detail. The same looseness appears in "weights, ranges, and thresholds" — "ranges" and "thresholds" are never described anywhere in the document.

findings.title: Tick determinism is not supported by the pluggable spatial query or by the stated precision policy
findings.description:
Two mechanisms contradict "Tick determinism — Given the same state and inputs, a tick produces the same outputs":

1. "Pluggable spatial queries" claims the strategy "can be replaced without changing the engine," and the 100 slice plan's (105) acceptance criterion is that output is "identical before and after the swap." Force accumulation is a floating-point reduction over neighbor order, and float addition is not associative, so brute force, spatial hash, KD-tree and GPU implementations will not produce bit-identical results unless the neighbor result set has a canonical order. Nothing in the document (or in the spatial interface contract as realized) mandates deterministic ordering (e.g., sorted indices) as part of the `SpatialQuery` contract. Either pin ordering in the interface or weaken the determinism claim.
2. "State serialization boundary" anticipates raw Float32 buffers for transfer while internal float64 is preferred, asserting the engine "should ... provide an efficient conversion path at the serialization boundary rather than compromising either concern." But determinism is motivated specifically by "eventual distribution (where regions must agree on simulation results from shared boundary state)." A lossy float64→float32→float64 round trip at a region boundary cannot reproduce the originating region's float64 trajectory, and the conversion is by definition not zero-copy. The document should state the precision policy as a decision (and where it applies) rather than deferring it while claiming cross-region agreement.

findings.title: No failure-mode or error strategy; the neighbor contract does not even define self-inclusion, which interacts catastrophically with the force set
findings.description: The only robustness statement in the entire document is a passing note that "Euler integration is simplest but can produce energy drift at high force magnitudes." There is no error-handling strategy for the tick: what happens when a force yields a non-finite value (with N agents in contiguous arrays, one NaN contaminates the whole population on the next tick), when two agents occupy the same position, when a profile is numerically invalid, or when a force implementation returns a wrong-shaped array. This collides with the project convention "Never use silent fallback values. Fail explicitly," and the pluggable-force contract makes third-party force implementations a first-class extension point, so failure attribution matters. A concrete instance is missing from the interface contract itself: the neighbor-query description ("which agents are within radius R of agent A") never states whether A is included in its own neighbor set. Self-inclusion is not a cosmetic detail — combined with the separation force the document endorses ("scaled inversely by distance," implemented as inverse-square falloff), an agent at distance 0 from itself produces 0/0. If an implementation follows the architecture's description without the self-exclusion rule that the slice layer had to invent, the result is NaN propagation across the state array, i.e. silent total corruption. The interface contract should specify self-inclusion and the tick should specify non-finite handling.

findings.title: Profile registry ownership, ordering, and runtime-mutation semantics are never stated
findings.description: "Profile as data" claims profiles "can be serialized, loaded from configuration, and swapped at runtime." Nothing in this document says who owns the profile collection, whether agent→profile binding is by identity or by position, or what happens to live agents when the set changes. In practice the binding is a positional integer index into a caller-owned ordered list (`profile_indices` in AgentState), which makes list ordering and stability a hard contract; the world server slice (303) has to flag exactly this as an operational risk ("The `SimulationManager` must receive profiles in the same order so that `profile_indices` in `AgentState` resolve correctly. The server is responsible for ensuring this alignment") and simultaneously defers "Dynamic profile changes at runtime" to future work. So the architecture advertises a runtime-mutation capability that no slice delivers and whose mechanics it never defines — including the determinism consequence, since a mid-run profile swap is a hidden input that must be captured for replay to reproduce a trajectory. State whether the profile list is append-only and immutable per run, or define the swap semantics (including replay logging) here.

findings.title: Reduced-rate ticking invariant for neighbor visibility is undefined
findings.description: Envisioned State, step 2 asserts the crucial contract: "Neighbors may include agents outside the active subset — an agent ticked at reduced rate is still visible to its neighbors." "Subset-evaluable tick" adds that the engine's tick "accepts an agent subset (index array or mask) to evaluate" and that the engine "does not decide which agents to evaluate — the caller does." What the document never states is whether the caller must keep inactive agents' positions current (e.g., ahead-interpolated) before the tick. If inactive agents simply retain their last-integrated position, they appear frozen for 3+ ticks, which measurably changes the emergent behavior of their active neighbors relative to full-fidelity simulation — undermining the world server's claim that the strategy "maintain[s] tick rate without sacrificing behavioral fidelity where it matters." This is a load-bearing precondition of the interface this document exists to define, and it also affects determinism/replay (interpolation is an input the log must capture). The document should state the position-currency invariant for inactive agents, or state explicitly that staleness is accepted.

findings.title: Tick contract is described inconsistently across the document
findings.description: Envisioned State describes the tick as a value-producing function ("Returns the updated state array"), and "Current State"/Overview frame the engine as "stateless between ticks ... No setup, no teardown, no mocks." The realized contract in slice 100 (and consumed by the world server in slice 303) is the opposite on both counts: `tick()` returns `None` and mutates `AgentState` in place, and it requires a stateful `SpatialQuery` instance whose `build(positions)` must be called each tick, plus an ordered profile list whose positional indices must align with `profile_indices`. "No setup, no teardown" is therefore inaccurate, and "returns the updated state array" will mislead any consumer reading only this document — especially a future region-partitioning implementation, where in-place mutation of canonical arrays versus returning new arrays is a meaningful difference. Align the prose with the interface that was actually established, or state that the interface is TBD.

findings.title: Broken cross-reference to the world server architecture
findings.description: Related Work cites "[200-arch.world-server-foundation.md](200-arch.world-server-foundation.md)" as the source for "detailed entity scaling tiers and multi-resolution simulation strategy that informs the engine's interface requirements." No such file exists; the document is `project-documents/user/architecture/300-arch.worldserver-foundation.md`. The same stale path is repeated in `100-slices.behavior-engine.md:43`. Since the scaling tiers (10K → 4M+) and the multi-resolution strategy cited throughout this document's Design Goals and Technical Considerations are load-bearing inputs to its interface requirements, a dead reference to that content is worth fixing before review of the derived slices.
